title: Opacity vs alpha
learningObjectives: Explain opacity vs alpha and apply it correctly in a small CSS example.

understand.concept: The opacity property applies transparency to an entire element, including its descendants and rendered content. Alpha in a colour value applies transparency to that particular colour. These approaches can produce different results when text, borders, and child elements are involved.
understand.whyItMatters: If a parent has opacity: .5, its whole rendered group is composited at half opacity. If only background-color has an alpha value, text can remain fully opaque. Opacity below 1 also creates a stacking context.
understand.analogy: A translucent window affects everything seen through it, while a transparent paint layer behind text can leave the text crisp. This is a visual comparison, not a complete explanation of browser compositing.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy helps build intuition, but the browser follows the CSS specifications and computed-style rules rather than human intentions.

explain.narrative: The first card fades both background and text. The second uses a translucent background while its text remains fully opaque.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to learn the effect of a CSS value?
options: Change one value and inspect the rendered result
Add unrelated declarations until it looks right
Assume every browser calculates styles identically in every context
questions.answer: Change one value and inspect the rendered result
questions.explanation: Controlled experiments make it easier to connect a CSS declaration with its visible effect.
